$comment: Elevator class reference data, plus one block that is not about a class: airPressure is a property of a shaft's travel rather than of a machine, and it is here because it is the same reference file every consumer already loads. See docs/02-elevator-reference.md for sources and rationale, including its Descent is capped by air pressure section.

conventions.$comment: designLoadFactor 0.8 is the universal traffic-analysis assumption: cars fill to 80% of rated capacity, not 100%. Using 1.0 makes the simulator systematically optimistic.

airPressure.$comment: AGENT'S PROPOSAL — GitHub issue #444. The descent limit air pressure imposes, and the equipment that lifts it. Read the MEASURED / CHOSEN split below field by field before treating any of it as a reference value; only one of the three numbers is cited. MEASURED (cited): descentCapMps 10.0, from Al-Kodmany, Buildings 2015, 5(3), 1070-1104, doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, s 3.1.4 verbatim — 'because of the air-pressure problem, elevators continue to descend not faster than 10 m per second'. The limit is on how fast a sealed cabin may shed ambient pressure without hurting the ears of the people inside, not on what the hoist can turn, which is why it is here rather than on a class and why it can be bought off. CHOSEN (an agent's, derived from the same paper and not stated by it): appliesAboveTravelM 300. The paper says passengers in very tall buildings 'might have just 30 s to adjust air pressure'; 30 s at the 10 m/s cap is 300 m of travel, so 300 is that sentence read as a distance. It is a round figure supporting a derivation, not a measurement, and the owner should read its consequence for the shipped set rather than the derivation: at 300 m exactly two shipped banks are above the threshold — vertical-city's shuttle at 307.5 m and burj-class-reference's shuttle and observation cars at 496.0 m — and every other bank in data/buildings/ is below it, the next highest being mixed-use-high-rise's shuttle at 126.0 m. So the threshold separates the two supertall towers from everything else, which is a game-design consequence and an owner's call: lower it towards ~120 m and the cap starts governing mixed-use-high-rise as well. CHOSEN (a refusal rather than a figure): pressurisedDescentCapMps null, meaning no cap at all. The paper records One World Trade Center answering the problem by pressurising the cars and releasing the pressure slowly, and Shanghai Tower fitting a pneumatic system; it records no residual speed limit for a pressurised cabin, so a number here would be invented. Null lets the machine's own rated speed bind again. NOT MEASURED and deliberately not modelled: the pressurisation kit's mass, its energy draw, and any effect on ascent. UNBOUND BY THIS BLOCK: every shipped car today. data/buildings/'s fastest is 10.0 m/s, which is exactly the cap, so no shipped run changes by a single leg — the block is a ceiling a player meets by buying past it, not a retrofit of the shipped towers.
airPressure.source: Al-Kodmany, K. (2015). Tall Buildings and Elevators: A Review of Recent Technological Advances. Buildings 5(3), 1070-1104, doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, s 3.1.4. descentCapMps is quoted from it; appliesAboveTravelM is an agent's proposal derived from the same section's '30 s to adjust' and is not a figure the paper states; pressurisedDescentCapMps is null because the paper records pressurisation as the answer to the problem rather than as a higher limit.

regenerativeDrive.$comment: AGENT'S PROPOSAL — GitHub issue #431, DECISIONS.md § D539. APPROVED AS DRAFTED by the product owner on 2026-09-11. What a regenerative drive returns when a bank fits one (buildings' banks[].regenerativeDrive). Read the CITED / CHOSEN split before treating the figure as a reference value: it is not one. CITED: the band the figure is derived from, Al-Kodmany, Buildings 2015, 5(3), 1070-1104, doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, s 2.1.4 verbatim — 'Generally, a regenerative drive can reduce energy consumption between 20% and 40%' — and the two cases a drive recovers from, same section, 'traveling up cars are light, or traveling down cars are heavy'. The paper gives no recovery efficiency, only that whole-consumption band. CHOSEN (an agent's, derived rather than measured): recoveryFraction 0.6. The energy proxy charges an overhauling move 1 - recoveryFraction of its out-of-balance work and a motoring move all of it, so the saving on a run is recoveryFraction times the overhauling share of that run's work. At the counterweight's default half-load balance that share is one half when traffic is symmetric, and 0.6 is the figure at which such a run saves 30 %, the middle of the paper's band. Real runs are not symmetric — an up-peak climbs with full cars and descends empty, both of which motor — so the saving a shipped contract actually shows is measured and published beside this figure in the PR that introduced it, rather than assumed from the derivation. The figure is game feel as much as physics, and the product owner approved it as drafted on 2026-09-11.
regenerativeDrive.source: Band cited from Al-Kodmany, K. (2015). Tall Buildings and Elevators: A Review of Recent Technological Advances. Buildings 5(3), 1070-1104, doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, section 2.1.4 (20%-40% whole-consumption reduction). The fraction itself is an agent's derivation from that band and is not stated by the source.

ropeClasses.$comment: AGENT'S PROPOSAL — GitHub issue #433, DECISIONS.md § D583. AWAITING THE PRODUCT OWNER'S APPROVAL; nothing here has been approved. The hoisting rope: what it weighs, and how far one hoistway may run on it. It sits beside the classes rather than inside one for airPressure's reason — a rope is a property of the shaft's travel and of what the operator bought, not of the machine class, and a bank buys a class of rope (buildings' banks[].ropeClass) exactly as it buys a regenerative drive. READ THE CITED / CHOSEN SPLIT FIELD BY FIELD BEFORE TREATING ANY FIGURE AS A REFERENCE VALUE. CITED, from Al-Kodmany, Buildings 2015, 5(3), 1070-1104, doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, s 2.1.5 verbatim: 'in very tall buildings, almost 70% of the elevator's weight is attributed to the cable itself, and when the rope gets too long it cannot support its own weight'; a steel installation with a 2000 kg car over 500 m of travel carries 'about 27,000 kg' of rope and KONE's carbon-fibre UltraRope 'about 2,500 kg' at the same travel; steel caps a single hoistway 'at roughly 500 m' and carbon fibre 'doubles it to 1000 m'. The same section records that UltraRope 'makes sense in buildings 200 m or taller' and that aramid (Schindler) and coated belt (Otis Gen2) 'sit in between' — with no figures for either, which is why two of the four rows below are wholly chosen. CHOSEN (an agent's, derived rather than measured): massKgPerMOfTravel for steel (54) and carbon-fibre (5) is the paper's own pair divided by the paper's own travel — 27000/500 and 2500/500. The division assumes rope mass is linear in travel, which is true of a hanging rope's length and is the only step the source does not take itself. It is the mass of ALL the rope that moves with one car at car speed — every fall, both sides of the sheave, and whatever compensation is fitted — because that is what the paper's 27,000 kg is. CHOSEN OUTRIGHT (no figure in the source, and the weakest two rows here): coated-belt at 32 kg/m and 600 m, and aramid at 16 kg/m and 750 m. The source says only that both 'sit in between'; the ORDER between them is chosen too — a coated belt keeps a steel cord inside a polyurethane jacket and is placed nearer steel, an aramid rope is a synthetic fibre and is placed nearer carbon. A reader who disagrees with either is disagreeing with a judgement, not correcting an error. WHAT THE CEILING DOES: maxSingleTravelM is a HARD REFUSAL, not an advisory. A bank that declares a rope class and spans further than that class allows fails to load with rope-travel-exceeds-class (core config/schema.ts#ISSUE_CODES). The lift class's own maxRiseM stays ADVISORY and is untouched — the product owner re-asked and reversed that on GitHub issue #433 on 2026-09-10, because hardening it reds midtown-office by 0.9 m. UNBOUND BY THIS BLOCK: every shipped building. No bank in data/buildings/ declares a ropeClass, so no shipped figure moves and no shipped run is refused. Measured rather than assumed: the tallest shipped single-hoistway travel is burj-class-reference's observation bank at 452.0 m, then its shuttle at 448.3 m and vertical-city's shuttle at 307.5 m — so even if every bank were given steel by default, none would reach steel's 500 m and none would be refused. The ceiling is proved by a test configuration that breaches it (core config/rope.test.ts), which is the amendment the owner gave this issue's third acceptance criterion on 2026-09-11. NOT MODELLED, deliberately and said here rather than discovered later: rope mass does not change a leg. It reaches the energy proxy as the kinetic energy of the moving rope and nothing else, so no car goes slower for being roped in steel, no dispatcher reads it, and Car.estimateCost() never sees it — see core metrics/types.ts#ropeInertiaWorkJ for what is charged and what is left out. The paper's 'about 15% energy reduction' is a claim about a whole installation's consumption and is NOT what this proxy measures; what the carbon option is worth here is measured and published in DECISIONS.md § D583 rather than quoted from the source.

classes.name: Steel wire rope
classes.application: The default of the industry and of this file's own reference classes. Heaviest, cheapest, and the constraint the whole block exists to express: at 500 m a single hoistway's rope weighs about what thirteen full cars do.

classes.name: Coated steel belt
classes.application: A steel cord in a polyurethane jacket (Otis Gen2 is the named example). Lighter than round rope and still steel inside, so it is placed nearest steel. CHOSEN: the source gives no figure.

classes.name: Aramid fibre rope
classes.application: A synthetic fibre rope (Schindler is the named example). CHOSEN: the source gives no figure.

classes.name: Carbon-fibre rope
classes.application: KONE UltraRope. The source says it 'makes sense in buildings 200 m or taller' and that it doubles the single-hoistway ceiling; below that rise it is mass and money spent on a shaft that had no rope problem.

ropeClasses.source: Al-Kodmany, K. (2015). Tall Buildings and Elevators: A Review of Recent Technological Advances. Buildings 5(3), 1070-1104, doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, section 2.1.5. The steel and carbon-fibre rope masses at 500 m and the 500 m / 1000 m single-hoistway ceilings are quoted from it; massKgPerMOfTravel is those masses divided by that travel, an agent's derivation the source does not state. The aramid and coated-belt rows are chosen outright — the source places both 'in between' and gives no figure for either.

passengerTransferS.$comment: Per passenger, per direction. ISO 4190-6 uses 1.75s for residential. CITED for hospital: CIBSE Guide D prices a bed or trolley transfer at roughly twice a passenger's, and a hospital car's population is a mix of ambulant visitors, staff and attended trolleys. 2.5 s is that mix, not a bed alone -- a bed-only car would be slower still. NOTE: this is the building-type DEFAULT. st-jude-hospital's bed bank overrides it to 3.0 s per car, which is how a building says its two banks carry different traffic; the default is what an unqualified hospital car gets.

loadSensor.$comment: Fractions of rated load. Bypass at 80% is the real production feature behind 'skip floors that have been called'.
